title: Assessing Alopecia Areata Misinformation: Social Media Analysis (Francis, Agarwal, Fanous, Siegel & Daneshjou, JMIR Dermatology 9:e90088, 2026)
screen_reason: Content analysis of 98 YouTube and 222 TikTok videos retrieved by #alopecia / #alopeciatreatment, each categorised against American Academy of Dermatology / National Alopecia Areata Foundation treatment guidelines, including an explicit 'misinformed and/or false' category. Shares of items classified false/inaccurate with stated denominators are reported for both platforms, meeting the CONTENT criterion.

missed_or_uncertain: Not extracted as prevalence: the 'limited or anecdotal evidence' category (YouTube 10%, n=10 of 98, i.e. 43% of the 23 treatment videos; TikTok 5%, n=12 of 222, i.e. 23% of the 52 treatment posts). By the protocol this is a QUALITY-style judgement - the paper defines it as 'unverified treatments without clear misinformation' and 'treatments with limited, inconsistent, or primarily anecdotal clinical support' - so it is not a falsity share, even though a single sentence in the Methods confusingly merges its definition with the 'misinformed and/or false' category. A broader 'not evidence-based' definition (misinformed + limited) would be a cross-category sum, which R8 forbids, so it was not computed. The 'accurate and medical data-backed' shares (13%/17% overall; 56%/73% among treatment videos) are accuracy, not misinformation, and their complements were not computed.

rob.design: Apify hashtag scrape of #alopecia / #alopeciatreatment over one week (17-24 July 2024); 98 YouTube and 222 TikTok videos; duplicates and non-English or advertisement posts excluded; manual relevance screening by one reviewer (SF) and content categorisation by a single reviewer with interrater reliability explicitly not calculated; chi-square comparison of platforms; engagement metrics not collected, so no view-weighting; no IRB review required (public data).
rob.item6_quote: Videos were categorized using standard AA treatment guidelines into (1) accurate and medical data-backed (aligned with guideline-supported treatments), (2) limited or anecdotal evidence (unverified treatments without clear misinformation), (3) misinformed and/or false (inaccurate or misleading claims), or (4) other (unrelated to alopecia management).
rob.item10_quote: Of the TikTok videos analyzed, 76% (n=170) were categorized as "other," 17% (n=38) as "accurate and medical data-backed," 5% (n=12) as "limited or anecdotal evidence," and 1% (n=2) as "misinformed and/or false."
